# Client fixtures

Shared test data for the aimux clients. `now/*.json` pins how the "Now" screen lays out sessions (the Mac's iTerm2 windows, tabs and panes, then folders), `search/*.json` the one search of Now and All, and `all/*.json` how the "All" screen lists them by day or as a folder tree, `chat/*.json` how a session's chat merges history turns and live events into display items, `terminal/*.json` how a message typed into a terminal on the Mac is recognised in the history and the words and codes of Open on Mac, `display/*.json` how a saved user message is shown in its bubble, `markdown/*.json` how Markdown text parses into the block tree both clients render, `references/*.json` how issue numbers, commits, Jira keys and file paths in that tree become links, and `media/*.json` how a paragraph that is only a link to a video, image or audio file becomes a media card, so the iPhone app (Swift Testing) and the web client (`node --test`) pass the same files. All titles, ids and paths are made up.

## Now (`now/*.json`)

Each file has `name`, `now` (the clock), `sessions` (the `Session` wire shape of the session list, including the optional `lastPrompt`, `description`, `pinned`, `folder`, `mac`, `working` and `waiting`), `events` (session id to a list in the events endpoint's wire shape, from which activity is derived), optionally `query` (the search box's text; absent is no query) and `workingOnly` (the Working chip; absent is `false`), and `expect`: `needsYou`, `pinned` and `other` (ordered ids), `windows` (ordered, each `{"id", "name", "tabs": [{"index", "name", "panes", "working", "open", "sessions": [ids]}]}`, tabs and sessions ordered), `hiddenTabs` (a number), `elsewhere` (ordered, each `{"label", "sessions": [ids]}`), and `working` and `open` (numbers); optionally `steps`, a map from session id to the expected working `step` (a string, or `null` for none), `descriptions`, a map from session id to the expected description line (a string, or `null` for none), and `rowStates`, a map from session id to the expected text of the row's state line (a string, or `null` for none), each compared for the sessions listed. Build Now with `now` as the clock and compare every field.

Activity per session, from its events ordered by `seq`: a pending approval (an `approval` with no later `approval_resolved` for its id) wins, and when a session has several the latest one wins; otherwise the last turn event (`turn_started`, `turn_done`, `turn_error`) decides: `turn_error` is failed (at its time), `turn_done` is finished (at its time), `turn_started` with no end is working; no turn events means no activity. The working `step` is found by walking the events of that turn from newest to oldest: the first `update` that is an `agent_thought_chunk` gives "Thinking", the first `tool_call` or `tool_call_update` with a title gives that title (an update with no title is skipped); whichever comes first from the end wins, and none means no step. A finish places nothing: a finished session is placed by its `state` like any other.

Open and working. A session is open when its `state` is `busy` or `open_in_terminal`, or its activity is working. It is working when its `state` is `busy`, its activity is working, or it has `working: true` (the server sends `working` only for a session open in a terminal whose Claude the registry calls busy). `lastActive` never makes a session open or working: a terminal session idle in its pane is open and not working, however recently it was active. Every other state (`idle`, `unavailable`, unknown ones) is closed unless the activity is working. A session with `mac` counts as open everywhere (Now's open count, Elsewhere's test and Search's Mac-order list), whatever its `state`. `working` and `open` in `expect` count the working and the open sessions among all of `sessions` (Needs you, pinned and filtered-out sessions included), before `query` and `workingOnly`; they are the Working chip's number and the open count.

Sections, top to bottom: Needs you, Pinned, the windows (On your Mac), Elsewhere and, with a query, Other sessions. A session appears at most once, in the first of these that takes it; Needs you wins over every other section. A session no section takes is not shown (without a query, every closed session that is neither in Needs you nor pinned).

- Needs you: pending approvals and sessions waiting for permission, together newest first, then failures of the last 900 s (newest failure first), whatever the session's `state`, `mac` or pin. A pending approval's time is its session's `lastActive` (an approval has no age of its own); a waiting session's (one with `waiting` of `kind` `permission`, which the server sends for a terminal session at a permission prompt) is `waiting.since`; a time after `now` counts as `now`, and equal times order by id ascending. A session with both is placed once, by its approval. A `waiting` that is absent, `null`, of another `kind` or without one places nothing and gives no waiting line. A failure older than 900 s places nothing. Approvals and waiting sessions are listed before failures whatever their times.
- Pinned: every session with `pinned: true` that is not in Needs you and has no `mac`, open or closed, whatever its state; newest first. A pinned session with `mac` stays in its pane (the row carries a pin mark) and is not listed in Pinned.
- Windows: every session with `mac` that is not in Needs you, whatever its state or pin. Sessions are grouped into windows by `mac.window.id`, ordered by `mac.window.index` ascending (ties by id ascending); a window's `id` and `name` are its sessions' `mac.window.id` and `mac.window.name`, used as sent (the owner's title or "Window N"; every session of a window carries the same values). Inside a window, sessions are grouped into tabs by `mac.tab.index`, ordered ascending; a tab's `name` is `mac.tab.name` and `panes` is `mac.panes` (the panes the tab has on the Mac, shells included, not the number of sessions listed; every session of a tab carries the same values). A tab's sessions are ordered by `mac.pane` ascending, ties by id. Window, tab and pane numbers compare as numbers (pane 10 comes after pane 9). A tab's `working` counts the working sessions it lists. A tab's `open` says whether it starts unfolded: `true` when one of the tab's sessions, before `query` and `workingOnly`, has `mac.lastInFront: true`, otherwise `false` (so with no such session every tab starts folded); with a query every tab shown is `true`. Folding a tab by hand and remembering it on the device are client state and not pinned, except the key: both clients remember a tab's fold under `<window name>|<tab index>|<tab name>` (the window's `name`, the tab's `index` and `name`, as sent, so two tabs with one name stay apart); a key stored in another form is ignored. A tab whose every session is in Needs you does not exist (and is not counted in `hiddenTabs`), nor does a window without tabs.
- Elsewhere: every open session with no `mac` that is not in Needs you or Pinned (started from the phone, in another terminal app, or open but not matched to a pane). Grouped by `folder.label`; a session with no `folder`, or whose `folder.label` is empty, uses the last component of its `project` (the text after its last `/`, trailing slashes trimmed first). Sessions with the same label are one group, whatever their `repoPath` (the server keeps labels distinct). Sessions newest first; groups ordered by their first session, newest first, ties by label ascending.
- Other sessions: only with a query, every matching session that is not open and not in Needs you or Pinned, newest first. Without a query `other` is `[]`.

When no session has `mac` (iTerm2 not running, Automation not granted), `windows` is `[]` and every open session that is not in Needs you or Pinned is in Elsewhere; the view may head that list "On your Mac" (not pinned).

Query. Lower-case the query (Unicode default lower-casing) and split it on whitespace into words; a query with no words (absent, empty or only whitespace) is no query. A word matches a session when it is a substring of one of the session's lower-cased `title`, `description`, `folder.label`, `mac.tab.name`, `mac.window.name` or `lastPrompt` (a missing field is empty text); a session matches when every word does, each word in any of those fields. Matching is plain substring: no word boundaries, no folding of accents. With a query, only matching sessions stay in every section, Needs you and Pinned included. A tab left with no session is left out and counted in `hiddenTabs`; a window left with no tab is left out (its tabs are counted); an Elsewhere group left with no session is left out and not counted.

Working only. With `workingOnly`, only working sessions stay in Pinned, the windows and Elsewhere; Needs you is kept whole, since a session waiting on the owner must stay in sight (a query still narrows it), and Other is empty (a closed session is never working). A tab left with no session is left out and counted in `hiddenTabs`, a window left with no tab is left out, and an Elsewhere group left empty is left out and not counted. A tab's `open` does not change with `workingOnly`. With both a query and `workingOnly` a session must pass both, and a tab left empty counts once. `hiddenTabs` is `0` with neither.

Order and time. "Newest first" orders by `lastActive`, where a `lastActive` after `now` counts as `now`, and equal times by id ascending. Ids and labels compare as plain strings, code point by code point (not locale collation). Timestamps keep every fractional digit the server sends (0 to 9), not just milliseconds, so events a fraction of a millisecond apart order by time and the 900 s window is measured exactly. Limits are inclusive (a failure exactly 900 s old counts).

Rows keep the session's own status (the dot) wherever they are; a session with `waiting` shows the needs-you dot. The state line is "Waiting for permission" for a session with `waiting`, whatever its activity; otherwise "Working" (with " · " and the step when there is one) for a working session, a "Your turn" line with the time since `lastActive` for an open one (its wording is the clients' and not pinned), and none for a closed one. All's rows show only the waiting line. The view shows a waiting session in Needs you as its session row (the chat's prompt card answers), and the chat's Next bar labels it "waiting for permission". The description line, where a row shows one, is the trimmed `description` when it has text, otherwise `null` (a missing, `null`, empty or blank value is `null`); trimming removes Unicode whitespace at both ends, and text inside is kept; truncation to one line is the view's job and is not pinned here. Two behaviours are the clients' and not pinned here: nothing reorders while the screen is open (status changes in place), and the layout shown is kept until `mac` has been absent for 30 s.

Files. `mac-order.json` (two windows listed out of order, numeric tab and pane order, a shell pane counted in `panes`), `window-renamed.json`, `last-in-front-opens-tab.json`, `no-last-in-front.json`, `unmatched-goes-elsewhere.json`, `pinned-open-stays-in-pane.json`, `pinned-closed.json`, `elsewhere-by-folder.json`, `empty-folder-label.json`, `needs-you-wins.json`, `working-only.json`, `query-hides-tabs.json`, `query-other-sessions.json`, `no-mac-at-all.json`; activity and Needs you: `approval-pending.json`, `approval-resolved.json`, `failed-recent.json`, `failed-old.json`, `boundary-900s.json`, `sub-millisecond.json`, `pinned-needs-approval.json`, `ties.json`; `clock-skew.json`, `terminal-active-and-idle.json` (recent activity is not working), `unknown-state.json`, `steps.json`, `descriptions.json`; waiting for permission: `waiting-terminal.json` (with approvals by time, before failures, Pinned and the windows; row states), `waiting-absent.json` (absent and `null` change nothing), `waiting-working-only.json` (kept by the Working chip, narrowed by a query), `waiting-unknown-kind.json` (another kind, or none, counts as no waiting).

## Search (`search/*.json`)

One search for Now and All: the box at the top of either screen matches on the device, as the owner types, over every session in the list. Each file has `name`, `now` (the clock), `query`, `sessions` (as in Now), optionally `events` (as in Now; absent means no activity) and `expect`: `{"open": [ids], "other": [ids]}`, both ordered. Words, matching and the open test are Now's. A query with no words gives `{"open": [], "other": []}` (the screen shows as usual, never blank). `open` lists the matching open sessions with `mac` in Mac order (`mac.window.index`, then `mac.window.id`, `mac.tab.index`, `mac.pane`, numbers as numbers, then id), then the matching open sessions without `mac`, newest first. `other` lists every other matching session, newest first. Needs you, pins and the Working chip play no part. On Now the same words drive the query rules above. The server's conversation search (`GET /v1/search`, after 400 ms) is listed after these under "In conversations" and is not pinned here.

Files. `title-and-label.json`, `tab-name.json` (tab and window names), `every-word.json`, `blank.json`, `open-first.json`.

## All (`all/*.json`)

Each file has `name`, `now` (the clock), `timeZone` (an IANA name such as `Europe/Berlin`; days are read in it), `project` (a session `project` path to filter by, or `null` for all), `sort` (`recent` or `folders`), `sessions` (the `Session` wire shape of the remote API) and `expect`. Filter first: keep a session only when `project` is `null` or equals the session's full `project` path (a prefix, a subfolder or another parent with the same folder name does not match). A session's time is its `lastActive`, and one after `now` counts as `now`; "newest first" orders by that time, equal times by session `id` ascending.

Recent. `expect` is `{"sections": [{"day", "ids"}]}`, an ordered list; compare `day` and the session ids of every section, in order. Empty input or a filter that matches nothing gives no sections. A session belongs to the calendar day of its time in `timeZone`; that day is named `today` when it is the day of `now` in `timeZone`, `yesterday` when it is the day before, and otherwise `YYYY-MM-DD` (zero-padded, in `timeZone`). Sections are ordered by day, newest day first, and empty days are left out. Inside a day sessions are newest first. `state` plays no part.

Folders. `expect` is `{"repos": [{"repoPath", "name", "count", "working", "open", "sessions": [ids], "worktrees": [{"name", "count", "working", "open", "sessions": [ids]}]}]}`, compared whole. A session belongs to the repo `folder.repoPath`, named `folder.repo`; a session with no `folder` belongs to the repo whose `repoPath` is its `project` and whose name is the last component of `project` (the text after its last `/`, trailing slashes trimmed first). Sessions are grouped by `repoPath`; a repo's `name` is that of its newest session (the server sends one name per `repoPath`). Inside a repo, a session with `folder.worktree` belongs to the worktree of that name, and the others (no `worktree`, and every session with no `folder`) are the main checkout, listed in the repo's own `sessions`, which come first on screen. `folder.sub` plays no part (a session in a subfolder is in its checkout). Repos are ordered by `name` compared case-insensitively (both lower-cased, then code point by code point, not locale collation, so `_x` comes before `a`), equal names by `repoPath` ascending; worktrees by `name` the same way, equal lower-cased names by `name` as written. Sessions in the repo's `sessions` and in each worktree are newest first. A repo's `count` and `working` cover all its sessions, worktrees included; a worktree's cover its own. Working is Now's test without activity: All files carry no `events`, so it is `state` `busy` or `working: true`, and activity is ignored here. `open` says whether a folder starts unfolded: `true` only on the repo holding the newest session of all (after the filter) and, when that session is in a worktree, on that worktree; every other repo and worktree is `false`. Opening and closing folders by hand and remembering it on the device, and remembering Recent or Folders (Recent the first time), are client state and not pinned. Empty input or a filter that matches nothing gives `{"repos": []}`; a repo without main-checkout sessions has `"sessions": []` and one without worktrees `"worktrees": []`. Days and `state` (other than for `working`) play no part.

Files. Recent: `recent-by-day.json`, `midnight-in-berlin.json`, `project-filter.json`; Folders: `folders-tree.json`, `folders-same-name.json`, `folders-no-folder-field.json`.

## Chat (`chat/*.json`)

Each file has `name`, `now` (a clock; no rule uses it yet, so no expected value depends on it, and it is kept for rules that may need it), `turns` (`SessionDetail.turns` of the remote API: `{number, time, user, reply, tools: [{name, snippet, ok}]}`, oldest first), `events` (an `EventPage.events` list: `{seq, turn, kind, time, data}`) and `expect`: `{"items": [...], "working": bool, "pendingApproval": string|null}`. Build the timeline and compare the whole result, items in order, with every field. Times are parsed like every other timestamp here (all fractional digits count).

Items. Every field is always present; a missing string on the wire is `""`.

- `{"kind": "user", "text"}`: a prompt. Left out when the text is empty.
- `{"kind": "thought", "text", "seconds"}`: one run of thought chunks, texts joined as they are.
- `{"kind": "steps", "count", "seconds", "filesChanged", "steps": [{"kind", "target", "status", "detail": {"input", "error", "old", "new"}}]}`: a group of tool calls. `count` is the number of steps; `filesChanged` the distinct `target`s of steps whose `kind` is `edit` (whatever their status, empty targets left out), in first-seen order.
- `{"kind": "plan", "done", "total", "entries": [{"text", "status"}]}`: `text` is the entry's `content`, `status` its `status` as sent; `total` counts the entries, `done` those with `status` `completed`.
- `{"kind": "reply", "text"}`: one run of message chunks, texts joined as they are.
- `{"kind": "approval", "approvalId", "title", "command", "options", "outcome"}`: `command` is `toolCall.rawInput.command` when that is a string, else `null`; `options` is the wire list with each option cut to `{optionId, name, kind}`; `outcome` is `null` until an `approval_resolved` for its id gives `allowed`, `denied` or `expired` (copied as sent); one with no `outcome` leaves it `null`, so the approval stays pending. Missing option fields are `""`.
- `{"kind": "error", "text"}`: a `turn_error`'s `error`. `{"kind": "stopped"}`: a `turn_done` whose `stopReason` is `cancelled`. Any other `turn_done` adds no item.

`seconds` is a number of whole seconds, `round(ms / 1000)` with halves rounded up (2.5 s is 3) and anything below 0 counted as 0, or `null` when it cannot be computed (including when either time does not parse). History items have `null`.

Step `detail`. Every step carries `detail` with all four strings always present (`""` when absent): `input` what the tool was asked to do, `error` why it failed, `old` and `new` the text an edit replaced and wrote. A step whose four strings are all empty has nothing to open. Text is kept whole, whitespace and line breaks included (a leading tab in `old` stays); the event stream does not bound live text, so the clients cap what they draw, not the timeline: at most 4000 characters of `input`, and 2000 of `error` and of each diff line, each cut followed by `…`. Characters are counted the same way in both clients: Unicode code points on the web (`Array.from`), Unicode scalars on the iPhone (`unicodeScalars`). History steps copy the tool's `detail` fields of the remote API (`input`, `error`, `old`, `new`; the whole `detail` may be missing). The server leaves out an `input` the step's snippet already shows (a Read's path, a Task's description, a Grep pattern shown as `/pattern/`), so such a step has nothing to open.

Live steps derive each field from one event of the step, never merging across events: the events are the `tool_call` and the `tool_call_update`s for its `toolCallId`, in `seq` order, and the latest one that qualifies wins entirely.

- `input`: the latest event whose `rawInput` is an object; use that object alone (keys of earlier `rawInput`s are not merged in). It is the first of `command`, `pattern`, `url`, `query`, `description`, `file_path` that is a non-empty string (non-strings and `""` are skipped), else `""`. An edit's `input` is therefore its `file_path`, by design.
- `old` and `new`: the latest event whose `content` is an array containing an item of `type` `diff`; with several diff items in that event the first wins. `old` is its `oldText` and `new` its `newText`, each `""` when missing or not a string, with no fallback to `rawInput`. Only when no event has a diff item, they come from the latest event whose `rawInput` is an object: `old` is `old_string` and `new` is `new_string`, each `""` when missing, and `rawInput.content` (a Write) fills `new` only when `new_string` is absent.
- A value that is not a string counts as missing (`""`): `rawInput.old_string`, `new_string` and `content`, and a diff item's `oldText` and `newText`. So a non-string `new_string` lets a string `content` fill `new`. Likewise, for `error`, a `content` item whose `content.text` is not a string is skipped.
- `error`: the latest event that carries a `content` array, taking the `content.text` of its items whose `type` is `content` and whose `content.type` is `text`, joined by `\n` (other items are skipped), and only when the step's final status is `failed`; otherwise `""`. A later `failed` update without `content` keeps the earlier text, and a call that failed and then completed has no error.

History turns. Each history turn gives, in order: `user` (if `user` is not empty), one `steps` (if `tools` is not empty) and `reply` (if `reply` is not empty). A history step's `kind` comes from the tool `name`: `Read` is `read`; `Edit`, `Write`, `MultiEdit` and `NotebookEdit` are `edit`; `Grep`, `Glob` and `WebSearch` are `search`; `Bash` is `run`; every other name is `other`. Its `target` is `snippet` (`""` when absent), its `status` `ok` when `ok` is true, else `failed`.

Turns from events. Events are taken in `seq` order (not array order); events with a repeated `seq` are kept once (the first copy in the list), since a reconnecting client may hand a snapshot that overlaps the stream. They are grouped by `turn`. A turn has ended when it has a `turn_done` or `turn_error`; its first such event is its end. The running turn is the turn of the last event (by `seq`) whose turn has not ended; there is at most one, and any other turn that has not ended is left out entirely. `working` is true when there is a running turn, even when its `turn_started` has aged out of the log. A turn is drawn from its own events like this:

1. An event that changes nothing is ignored: it ends no run and times nothing. These are: an `update` whose `sessionUpdate` is none of `agent_message_chunk`, `agent_thought_chunk`, `tool_call`, `tool_call_update`, `plan`; a chunk whose `content` is not `{type: "text"}` with a non-empty `text`; a `tool_call_update` whose `toolCallId` has no step in this turn; an `approval_resolved` whose `approvalId` has no approval item in the timeline; and any event of an unknown `kind`.
2. `turn_started` adds `user` with its `text` (a missing `data` or `text` counts as `""`, so no item; prompt matching then uses `""`).
3. Chunk runs: `agent_thought_chunk`s with no other (non-ignored) event between them make one `thought`; `agent_message_chunk`s likewise make one `reply`. A run ends at the first non-ignored event of another kind, including `turn_done` and `turn_error`. A thought's `seconds` runs from its first chunk's time to the time of the event that ended its run, and is `null` while nothing has ended it.
4. Steps: a `tool_call` with a new `toolCallId` adds a step to the turn's current steps group, or, when there is none, appends a new group item at the end and makes it current. Appending a `reply` item ends the current group; thoughts, plans and approvals do not, so a tool call after them still joins the group above them. Step `kind` from the ACP `kind`: `read`, `edit` and `search` as they are, `execute` is `run`, anything else (or none) is `other`. `target` is the `title` (`""` when none). `status`: `completed` is `ok`, `failed` is `failed`, anything else (`pending`, `in_progress`, none) is `running`. A `tool_call_update`, or a `tool_call` repeating a known `toolCallId`, changes that step in place: a non-empty `title` replaces the target (an untitled update keeps it), a `kind` or `status` it carries replaces those. A group's `seconds` runs from the time of its first `tool_call` to the time of the last (by `seq`) `tool_call` or update that touched one of its steps (0 for a single call).
5. `plan`: the first one appends a plan item; later ones in the same turn replace its entries in place, so a turn has one plan at the position of its first.
6. `approval` appends an approval item; `approval_resolved` sets the `outcome` of the item with that `approvalId`, wherever it is.

Prompts match (`samePrompt(history, text)`) when the history `user`, with every run of whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines) folded to one space, ends trimmed and one trailing `…` (U+2026) removed, is not empty and is a prefix of the event `text` folded and trimmed the same way.

Merge. Windows are inclusive, 2 s wide.

1. The running turn may already be the latest history turn (the session file is written as the turn goes): when the running turn's first event (by `seq`) is its `turn_started` and the last history turn's prompt matches its `text` with a `time` no earlier than 2 s before the `turn_started`, that history turn is dropped. When the `turn_started` has aged out, nothing is dropped: history keeps the turn's first part and its retained events continue it.
2. Ended turns are placed in the order of their end events' `seq`. Each history turn can be claimed by one ended turn. With a `turn_started`, an ended turn claims the first unclaimed history turn whose prompt matches and whose `time` is between 2 s before the `turn_started` and 2 s after the end. Without one, it claims the latest unclaimed history turn whose `time` is at most 2 s after the end.
3. A turn that claimed a history turn adds only its terminal item (`error`, `stopped`, or nothing) right after that history turn's items; its other events are not repeated.
4. An ended turn with a `turn_started` that claimed nothing was never written to history: it is drawn from its events, followed by its terminal item. It is left out when history is not empty and its `turn_started` is earlier than the first history turn's `time`; otherwise it goes right after history turn k-1, where k is the first history turn whose `time` is later than its `turn_started`, and after all history when no history turn is later.
5. An ended turn with no `turn_started` that claimed nothing adds its terminal item after all history when history is empty or its end is no earlier than the first history turn's `time`, and nothing otherwise.

Order of the result: each history turn's items followed by what was placed after it (in placement order), then what was placed after all history, then the running turn drawn from its events (with no `user` item when its start aged out). `pendingApproval` is the `approvalId` of the last approval item in that order whose `outcome` is `null`, or `null`.

## Terminal (`terminal/saved-prompt-match.json`)

`cases` is a list of `{name, saved, pending, match}`: `saved` is a history turn's `user` as Claude Code saved it, `pending` the message the phone typed into the terminal, and `match` whether that history turn shows the message (so the pending line clears). Rules. Unwrap `saved` first: trim surrounding whitespace, drop a leading `The user sent a new message while you were working:`, remove every `<pasted_content>` and `</pasted_content>` tag (the opening tag may carry attributes, as in `<pasted_content id="6981">`; the text between them stays), trim again (the prefix and the tags are the shapes expected for messages typed while busy and long pastes; not yet seen in a live check). A message holding Claude Code's command tags is then taken in the form it was typed: split it into parts as in Display below (without removing image placeholders) and join, with a newline, each text part, each command as its name, then a space and its args when it has args (so `/compact` or `/tidy keep it short`), and each bash command as `!` and its input; outputs are left out, so a message that held only output or a caveat matches nothing. Then compare with the chat's `samePrompt(history, text)` above (whitespace folded, the unwrapped `saved` a non-empty prefix of `pending`).

## Open on Mac (`terminal/open-on-mac.json`)

The words and codes of Open on Mac (`POST /v1/sessions/{id}/open-on-mac`), shown when health has `openOnMac` true. `copy` maps a key to the exact text both clients show: `action` (the button), `progress` (while the request runs), `done` (after `200`), and one entry per refusal, keyed by the error `code` the server answers (`busy`, `open_in_terminal`, `in_use`, `not_started`, `no_terminal`, `not_authorized`, `timeout`). `success` is the `200` answer (`status` and the body's `state`). `codes` maps every error code the route answers to its HTTP status; `unknown_session` has no copy of its own (the clients' usual missing-session handling applies). The server's tests read this file too, so a code or status here is what the route answers.

## Display (`display/user-bubble.json`)

`cases` is a list of `{name, saved, display: {text, images, parts}}`: `saved` is a history turn's `user` as Claude Code saved it, `display.text` what goes to the bubble renderer (Markdown with typed line breaks kept, shown inline-only: every block becomes paragraphs) and `display.images` how many "Image" chips the bubble shows. Rules. Unwrap `saved` with the Terminal rules above (the same function the pending match uses), then remove every image placeholder: `[Image #n]` (`n` one or more digits `0-9`) and `[Image: …]` (any characters but `]` and a newline, up to the first `]`); case matters, so `[image #1]` stays. Each placeholder goes with the spaces and tabs right after it; a line that held a placeholder and is left with only spaces and tabs is dropped whole (its newline too); spaces and tabs at the end of such a line are dropped; then the text is trimmed. Every removed placeholder, in order, is one chip: a glyph and "Image n" for `[Image #n]` (the digits as written), "Image" for `[Image: …]`. The chips sit above the text; a bubble with no text and no chips is not shown. This applies to every `user` item of the timeline (a message typed on the phone has no wrappers, so nothing changes for it), not to the pending message.

Commands and their output. After unwrapping, the message is split into `parts`, in order: `{"kind": "text", "text"}`, `{"kind": "command", "text", "args"}` and `{"kind": "output", "text", "error"}`. A fixture case may leave `parts` out; it is then `[{"kind": "text", "text": <display.text>}]`, or `[]` when `display.text` is empty. Claude Code wraps a slash command, bash mode and their output in these tags, each written exactly like this, without attributes, and closed by the first matching closing tag (what is between them is taken as it is, never searched for more tags): `<command-name>`, `<command-message>`, `<command-args>`, `<local-command-stdout>`, `<local-command-stderr>`, `<command-stdout>`, `<command-stderr>`, `<bash-input>`, `<bash-stdout>`, `<bash-stderr>` and `<local-command-caveat>`. An opening tag with no closing tag after it, any other tag, and a closing tag on its own are text.

- `<command-name>` is a command: its content, trimmed, is `text` (with its leading `/`, as saved) and `args` is `""`. Empty content makes no part.
- `<command-args>` gives its content, trimmed, as the `args` of the command just before it, when that command came from `<command-name>`, has no args yet and nothing but whitespace and dropped tags lies between them; otherwise its content is text, part of the text around it.
- `<bash-input>` is a command whose `text` is `!` and the content trimmed (Claude Code's bash mode), with `args` `""`; empty content makes no part.
- `<local-command-stdout>`, `<command-stdout>` and `<bash-stdout>` are an output with `error` `false`; the three `stderr` tags an output with `error` `true`. Its `text` is the content with every ANSI colour code (`ESC [`, digits and `;`, then `m`) removed, then trimmed; an output left empty makes no part.
- `<command-message>` (the command's name again, without the `/`) and `<local-command-caveat>` are dropped with their content.
- The text between two commands or outputs (or before the first, or after the last) is one text run, with the dropped tags taken out and nothing put in their place; each run has its image placeholders removed as above and is trimmed, and a run left empty is no part. `display.text` is the text parts joined by a blank line (`\n\n`); the chips count the placeholders of every text run. The bubble is shown when it has a part or a chip.

The bubble draws its parts in order: text as above; a command in monospace, its args after it as plain text (no Markdown); an output as a monospace block of plain text with its line breaks, and an error output labelled "Error output". Nothing in a command or an output is read as Markdown or HTML. Shapes seen in Claude Code transcripts: a command as `<command-name>`, `<command-message>`, `<command-args>` on three lines (or `<command-message>` first, and `<command-args>` absent), a command's output in a separate message as `<local-command-stdout>` (sometimes with colour codes), a separate `<local-command-caveat>` message before it, `<bash-input>` alone, and `<bash-stdout>` followed by `<bash-stderr>` (one of them usually empty) in the next message. `<local-command-stderr>`, `<command-stdout>` and `<command-stderr>` were not seen.

Other chat items (not pinned by a fixture). A `thought`'s text, each `plan` entry's `text`, each step's `target` and an `error`'s `text` go through the same inline-only Markdown with the references pass and the session's context, so code spans, emphasis, links, issue numbers and paths show as in a bubble. A step target with no whitespace and no backtick (a path, a pattern, a word) is not parsed as Markdown, so `pkg/__init__.py` keeps its underscores and `**/*.go` its stars; when it is a path as a whole (the `code` rule of References, applied to the whole target) it is that path reference, drawn in the step's own monospace without the code fill. Any other target is parsed, its lines and blocks joined by spaces. Step targets stay on one line (cut in the middle on the iPhone, with an ellipsis at the end on the web).

## Markdown (`markdown/*.json`)

Each file has `name`, `markdown` (the source text) and `blocks`, the normalized block tree that both clients must produce from it. Parse `markdown` and compare the whole tree, blocks in order, with every field. The dialect is GitHub-flavoured Markdown as Claude Code writes it; where nothing below says otherwise, CommonMark 0.31 and the GFM spec decide. The tree keeps only what both parsers can see: the web client parses with its own CommonMark parser, the iPhone app normalizes Foundation's `AttributedString(markdown:, interpretedSyntax: .full)`, and the rules below (alignment, no tightness, flat link text, canonical emphasis nesting, empty fences) are chosen so both reach the same tree. Fixtures pin each rule below unless the rule says it is not pinned.

Blocks. Every field is always present.

- `{"type": "heading", "level": 1-6, "inlines"}`
- `{"type": "paragraph", "inlines"}`
- `{"type": "list", "ordered", "start", "items": [{"task", "blocks"}]}`: `start` is the first item's number for an ordered list and `null` for a bullet list; `task` is `null` for a plain item, `false` for `[ ]`, `true` for `[x]` or `[X]`. A nested list is a `list` block inside an item's `blocks`. Item text is always a `paragraph` block; there is no tight or loose flag, rendering decides the spacing. An empty item has `"blocks": []`.
- `{"type": "code", "lang", "text"}`: `lang` is a string or `null`; `text` is the content without the trailing newline.
- `{"type": "quote", "blocks"}`
- `{"type": "table", "align", "header", "rows"}`: `align` has one entry per column, `"left"`, `"center"` or `"right"`; `header` is a list of cells and `rows` a list of rows, each a list of cells; a cell is a list of inlines (`[]` when empty).
- `{"type": "rule"}`

Inlines: `{"t": "text", "v"}`, `{"t": "code", "v"}`, `{"t": "em", "c"}`, `{"t": "strong", "c"}`, `{"t": "del", "c"}`, `{"t": "link", "href", "c"}`, `{"t": "br"}`, where `c` is a list of inlines; a link's `c` is always exactly one `text`. Two `text` inlines are never adjacent: runs that meet (after escapes, entities, dropped links and literal delimiters) are merged into one, and empty text is left out.

Block rules.

- ATX headings: 1 to 6 `#` then a space or tab (or end of line); 7 `#` or no space is paragraph text. A closing run of `#` preceded by a space is dropped, and the content is trimmed.
- Setext headings (CommonMark): paragraph text directly followed by a line of `=` (any number) is a level 1 heading, by a line of `-` (any number, including one) a level 2 heading; all the paragraph's lines make the heading, joined by a space. So `Steps:` followed by `-` is a level 2 heading `Steps:`, not a paragraph and an empty list item (`headings-setext.json`; micromark, commonmark.js and Foundation agree). A blank line before `---` makes it a rule.
- Paragraphs: lines are joined; a line break inside a paragraph (soft break) becomes one space, with the spaces and tabs at the end of the line and at the start of the next dropped. A hard break is a line ending in two or more spaces or in a backslash, and becomes `{"t": "br"}`; at the end of a paragraph or heading neither makes a `br` (the spaces are dropped). Paragraph content is trimmed.
- Indented code (4 spaces, not continuing a paragraph) is a CommonMark `code` block with `lang` `null`. Not pinned (Claude does not emit it).
- Lists: bullets `-`, `*`, `+`; ordered markers are 1 to 9 digits then `.` or `)`. A marker is followed by 1 to 4 spaces (or end of line), and the item's content column is just after them; a following line belongs to the item when it is indented to at least that column (or is a lazy paragraph continuation, below). So a child of `1. ` needs 3 spaces and a child of `- ` 2; `1. first` then `  - x` (2 spaces) is a new top-level bullet list, not a child. A different bullet character or a different ordered delimiter starts a new list, even without a blank line; ordered numbers after the first do not matter, and a blank line between items does not end a list. A list may interrupt a paragraph (an ordered one only when it starts at 1).
- Task items: an item whose content starts with `[ ]`, `[x]` or `[X]` followed by a space or tab is a task; the marker and that one space are removed from the item's first paragraph. `[ ]` with no space after it is text. Escaped brackets (`- \[ ] x`) are not pinned.
- Fenced code: 3 or more backticks or tildes, indented at most 3 spaces; it closes at a line of the same character at least as long as the opener, with nothing but spaces after it. The info string is trimmed and its first word (up to a space or tab) is `lang`; no info string is `null`; a backtick opener whose info string contains a backtick is not a fence. Content lines lose up to as many leading spaces as the opening fence was indented (inside a list item, the item's content column is removed first). A fence that is never closed runs to the end of its container (the end of the text, for a top-level fence). A fence with no content lines (closed or not) is left out of the tree (`stream-empty-fence.json`). Nothing inside code is parsed.
- Block quotes: lines starting with `>` (one optional space after it is removed); `>` inside a quote nests. A line without `>` that would continue the quote's open paragraph is a lazy continuation and joins that paragraph; a blank line ends the quote.
- Tables (GFM): a header row, then an alignment row of cells made of `-` with an optional `:` at either end (`:---` left, `:--:` center, `---:` right, and `---` with no colon also left), with as many cells as the header; otherwise the lines are paragraph text. Leading and trailing pipes are optional. Every following line is a row until a blank line or the start of another block. Cells are split on unescaped `|`, trimmed, and parsed as inlines; `\|` is a literal pipe, also inside a code span in a cell. A row with fewer cells than the header is padded with empty cells `[]`; extra cells are dropped.
- Rules: a line of 3 or more `-`, `*` or `_` (the same character, spaces between allowed), indented at most 3 spaces, not directly under paragraph text when it is `-` (that is a Setext heading). A rule wins over a list item (`- - -` is a rule); `***` directly under paragraph text is a rule.
- Raw HTML is never interpreted. A tag on its own line or inside a paragraph is literal text (`<script>alert(1)</script>` is the text `<script>alert(1)</script>`; pinned in `hostile.json`). Multi-line HTML is always literal text, never interpreted; how it splits into blocks is not pinned.
- Not pinned: reference-style links and definitions, footnotes, indented code, multi-line HTML layout, escaped task brackets, a trailing empty list item, an empty heading (`#` alone), a trailing table row whose cells are all empty, same-style nested emphasis (`*a *b* c*`), percent-encoding of an `href` holding non-ASCII characters or characters such as `|` (compare `href` only for ASCII-safe URLs), a link with empty text (`[](https://...)`: the web client shows its `href`, Foundation leaves nothing), an empty first item of an ordered list (`1. ` then `2. b`), a task marker with nothing after it (`- [ ] `), an explicit autolink ending in punctuation (`<https://example.com/a.>` may lose its `.`), and entity names beyond the common ones (`&amp;`, `&lt;`, `&gt;`, `&quot;`, `&copy;`, numeric references). An image with empty alt text is dropped (it leaves no text); not pinned. Nesting is bounded so that hostile text cannot exhaust a client: quotes and lists nest at most 100 levels, and a link destination holds at most 32 levels of nested parentheses (cmark's limit). What a client shows beyond depth 100 is not pinned (the web client keeps a deeper `>` or list marker as paragraph text; the iPhone app keeps the content in the 100th level without the markers). A client may show text longer than 256 KiB as plain preformatted text without parsing it, since a streaming reply is parsed again on every update; not pinned above 256 KiB.

Inline rules.

- Backslash escapes: a backslash before ASCII punctuation gives that character as text (`\*` is `*`); before anything else it is a literal backslash.
- Entities: named (`&amp;`, `&copy;`, `&lt;`, ...), decimal (`&#35;`) and hex (`&#x41;`) references decode to their characters as text, so `&lt;b&gt;` is the text `<b>`, never a tag. Unknown names stay literal. Entities are decoded in text and in link destinations, not in code.
- Code spans: a run of N backticks up to the next run of exactly N; inside, line breaks become spaces and, when the content both starts and ends with a space and is not all spaces, one space is removed from each end. An unmatched backtick run is literal text. Nothing inside a code span is parsed (no emphasis, links or URLs).
- Emphasis is parsed by the CommonMark delimiter-run rules: `*x*` and `_x_` are `em`, `**x**` and `__x__` are `strong`. A delimiter run followed by whitespace cannot open, preceded by whitespace cannot close (`** spaced **` is text). `_` cannot open or close inside a word, so `snake_case_word` is text; `*` can (`Intra*word*` is `em`). Delimiters that find no partner stay literal text.
- Strikethrough (GFM, cmark-gfm default): `~~x~~` and `~x~` are `del`.
- Canonical nesting (`emphasis-canonical.json`). After parsing, the inline content is flattened into leaves (text, code, link, br), each carrying the set of `em`, `strong` and `del` around it, and rebuilt: at each position, of the styles the leaf has that are not already open, the one whose run of consecutive leaves reaches furthest is opened outermost and covers exactly that run; on a tie `em` goes outside `strong`, which goes outside `del`. Inside it the same rule applies to the remaining styles, then text is merged again. So `**_x_**` and `***y***` are both `em` holding `strong`, and `~~**z**~~` is `strong` holding `del`.
- Links: `[text](destination)` and `[text](destination "title")` (the title is dropped); the destination may be wrapped in `<...>` and may contain balanced parentheses. A link's `c` is its text flattened to one `text` (emphasis and code inside the link text keep their characters and lose their styling: `[with **bold**](...)` has `c` `[{"t": "text", "v": "with bold"}]`); emphasis around a link is kept. Autolinks: `<scheme:...>` with no spaces or `<` `>` inside. Images `![alt](src)` are not shown: they become their alt text, except that a paragraph whose only content is one image with an `http:` or `https:` source is that image as a link: `{"t": "link", "href": src, "c": [{"t": "text", "v": alt}]}`, with the alt text flattened like a link's and the source as the text when the alt text is empty (so the media pass, below, can make it a card; a source that is no media address stays a link showing the alt text). Emphasis around the image, other text beside it or another scheme keeps the alt text.
- Scheme filter: a link (inline, autolink or bare URL) becomes `{"t": "link"}` only when its destination starts with `http:` or `https:` (case-insensitive); otherwise its content is spliced in as ordinary inlines (an autolink's content is the URL text without the angle brackets), so `[x](javascript:alert(1))` is the text `x` and relative, `mailto:` and `data:` links are text. `href` is the destination after escapes and entities are decoded, with no other normalisation.
- Bare URLs (cmark-gfm behaviour) are found in `text` leaves after emphasis and entities are resolved, never in code or inside another link. One starts with `http://` or `https://`, scheme matched case-insensitively (`HTTPS://` links, and `href` keeps the text as written), wherever it is not preceded by an ASCII letter: at the start of a leaf or after whitespace, `(`, a quote, `:`, a digit or other punctuation, but not inside a word (`abchttps://...` is text). It runs up to the next whitespace or `<` (or the end of the leaf). Then, repeatedly, a trailing `.`, `,`, `;`, `:`, `!`, `?`, `*`, `_`, `~`, `'` or `"` is cut off, and a trailing `)` is cut off when the URL has more `)` than `(`; what remains must have at least one character after `://`. Since entities are decoded first, `&amp;` inside a bare URL is `&` in both its text and its `href`. So `(see https://example.com/x)` links `https://example.com/x`, `"https://example.com/q"` links without the quotes, `https://example.com/wiki/Thing_(disambiguation)` keeps its `)`, and `**https://example.com/x**` is `strong` holding the link. The link's `c` is one `text` with the URL. `www.` addresses and email addresses are never links.

Streaming. A reply is re-parsed from its full text as each chunk arrives, so every prefix must parse without failing and the rules above give the result; no state is kept between prefixes. This means: an unclosed fence is code to the end of the text (`stream-unclosed-fence.json`), and a fence with no content line yet is left out (`stream-empty-fence.json`); a table appears once its header and an alignment row with as many cells as the header are there, and a partial last row is padded (`stream-partial-table.json`), while a header with an unfinished alignment row is still paragraph text; an unclosed `**`, `~~`, `*` or `[text](` stays literal text until its closer arrives (`stream-open-emphasis.json`); a line of `-` under a paragraph line, even a lone `-` just typed to start a list (or `- ` with its trailing space), makes that line a heading until the item's text arrives (`headings-setext.json`); a URL is linked as far as it has arrived.

## References (`references/*.json`)

Each file has `name` and `cases`, a list of `{name, context, inlines, expect}`. `inlines` is an inline list of the Markdown tree above; `expect` is that list after the references pass. `context` is what the client knows about the session: `repo` (`{web, branch, root}` from `SessionDetail.repo`, or `null`; `root` may be absent), `jiraBase` (`Health.links.jiraBase`, or `null`), `jiraProjects` (`Health.links.jiraProjects`, `[]` when absent) and `project` (the session's `project` folder, or `null`; a session started in a subfolder of the repository has a `project` below `repo.root`). Apply the pass to the `inlines` of every block that has them (paragraphs, headings, table cells) and compare the whole list.

The pass runs after the Markdown tree is built; `ref` inlines are produced only by it and never by the Markdown parser. A `ref` is `{"t": "ref", "kind": "pr" | "commit" | "jira" | "path", "v", "href"}`, where `v` is the matched text exactly as written and `href` the link target. A path that came from an inline code span adds `"code": true` (absent otherwise), so the client keeps the monospace look. The kind `url` is not produced: a bare `http(s)` URL is already a `link` in the tree. The visible text never changes (the concatenated `v` of `expect` equals that of `inlines`), `text` inlines are split around each `ref`, and the "no two adjacent `text`, no empty `text`" rule still holds.

Where it applies. To the `v` of `text` inlines, and inside the `c` of `em`, `strong` and `del`. Never inside a `link`, and never inside a `code` inline, except that a `code` inline whose whole `v` is a path (below) becomes a `ref` with `code: true`. A `text` inline is scanned alone: its start and end count as the start and end of the text. When a candidate cannot get a target (the context lacks what it needs), it stays text.

Scanning. Go left to right; at each position take the longest match of the rules below (ties: the order they are listed in), emit it, and continue after it; with no match, move one character on. "Word character" means `A-Z a-z 0-9 _`. "Boundary" means the next character is not a word character, or the text ends.

- Issue or pull request, `#123`: `#` and 1 to 6 digits, at the start or after whitespace or `(`, then a boundary. Needs `repo`. Not a reference when the whitespace-separated word before it (lowercased, leading `(`, `[`, `"` or `'` dropped) is `step`, `item`, `option`, `line`, `no.` or `number`, so `step #1` is text; a `#` right after `(` or at the start has no such word. `href` is `{repo.web}/issues/123`, on GitLab `{repo.web}/-/issues/123`. GitHub redirects an issue number to its pull request.
- Other repository, `owner/repo#123`: owner and repo are `A-Za-z0-9` followed by any of `A-Za-z0-9_.-`, then `#` and 1 to 6 digits, same start and boundary rule, no word list. Needs `repo` for the host: `href` is `{scheme and host of repo.web}/{owner}/{repo}/issues/123` (GitLab: `/-/issues/123`).
- Commit: 7 to 40 characters of `0-9a-f` as a whole word (not preceded by a word character, and a boundary after), with at least one digit and at least one letter. Needs `repo`. `href` is `{repo.web}/commit/{sha}`, GitLab `{repo.web}/-/commit/{sha}`. Uppercase never matches.
- Jira: `[A-Z][A-Z0-9]+-[0-9]+` as a whole word whose part before the `-` is in `jiraProjects`, with `jiraBase` set. `href` is `{jiraBase}/browse/{KEY}` (trailing `/` of the base dropped). An empty `jiraProjects` links nothing, so `UTF-8` and `ISO-9001` stay text.
- Path: one or more `/`-separated segments of `A-Za-z0-9_.@+-` ending in a file name whose extension is `.` then a letter and up to 9 letters or digits (so `3.4` is not one); a leading `/` is allowed. The matched text, which for an absolute path includes the root, has at least one `/`; after the root is removed a file directly in the root (`main.go`) is fine. The whole run of `A-Za-z0-9_.@+-` and `/` characters must be the path: a name glued on after the extension (`src/a.go_test`, `pkg/x.go-old`) makes it text, while a trailing period is sentence punctuation. It must not follow a word character or any of `/ . - @ + ~ :`. Trailing `.` characters are not part of it (`src/a.go.` is `src/a.go` and a period). Right after it, `:` and 1 to 6 digits followed by a boundary is its line. Needs `repo`. The repository-relative path is built as: an absolute path (starting `/`) counts only when it starts with `repo.root` plus `/` (`project` when `root` is absent), and that prefix is removed; trailing `/` characters of the root or project are ignored (any other absolute path stays text); a leading `./` is dropped. It stays text when any segment is `..` or empty, or when the first of several segments has a `.` that is not its first character (`example.com/a/b.html` is a web address, not a file; `.github/ci.yml` is a file). `href` is `{repo.web}/blob/{branch}/{path}`, plus `#L{line}` with a line; GitLab uses `{repo.web}/-/blob/{branch}/{path}`. The branch is used as written (`feature/ttl` keeps its slash). A `code` inline whose whole `v` is such a path, with an optional `:line`, becomes `{"t": "ref", "kind": "path", "v", "href", "code": true}`; anything else in code (a command, extra spaces) stays `code`.

GitLab means the host of `repo.web` contains `gitlab` (`gitlab.com` and self-hosted servers such as `gitlab.example.com`, with sub-groups in the path). The server reports `repo` only for `github.com` and such GitLab hosts.

Files. `prs.json`, `commits.json`, `jira.json` and `paths.json` pin each rule; `gitlab.json` the `/-/` forms; `no-context.json` that nothing links without `repo` or Jira settings; `false-positives.json` look-alikes (`step #1`, `deadbeef`, `UTF-8`, a path with no extension) that stay text.

## Media (`media/*.json`)

Each file has `name` and `cases`, a list of `{name, markdown, blocks}`. Parse `markdown`, run the references pass with no context (it changes nothing), then the media pass, and compare the whole tree with `blocks`. The media pass runs after references, on a reply's tree only (a user's message keeps its links).

A paragraph whose `inlines` are exactly one `link` (nothing else, not inside emphasis) whose `href` is a media address becomes `{"type": "media", "kind", "href", "title"}`, in place of the paragraph. This applies to paragraphs at any depth (inside quotes and list items), never to headings or table cells. Since paragraph content is trimmed, spaces around the link do not matter; a bare URL, an autolink, an inline link and an image alone in its paragraph (above) all give such a link. A link inside prose, two links, or a link in emphasis stays a link.

Media address. Split `href` (always `http:` or `https:`, scheme any case) into the host (the part after `://` up to the next `/`, `?` or `#`, less anything up to an `@` and a `:port`, lowercased) and the path (from that `/` up to the first `?` or `#`, empty when there is none); the query is what follows `?` up to `#`. Then, first match wins:

- `youtube`: host `youtube.com`, `www.youtube.com` or `m.youtube.com` with path `/watch` and a query parameter `v` (split on `&`) with a non-empty value, or a path `/shorts/` followed by a segment with no further `/`; or host `youtu.be` with a path `/` followed by a segment with no further `/`.
- `vimeo`: host `vimeo.com` or `www.vimeo.com` with a path of `/` and digits only.
- By the extension of the path's last segment (the text after its last `.`, compared lowercased; a path ending in `/` has an empty last segment and no extension): `video` for `mp4`, `mov`, `m4v`, `webm`; `image` for `png`, `jpg`, `jpeg`, `gif`, `webp`; `audio` for `mp3`, `m4a`, `wav`.

An `href` with a `\` or a `%5C` (any case) before the path (in the part after `://` up to the first `/`, `?` or `#`), or whose host as the client's URL parser reads it (a browser's `new URL(href).hostname`; Foundation's `URL(string:)?.host`, lowercased) differs from the split host, is not a media address and stays a link: a browser reads `\` as `/`, so `https://evil.example\@youtube.com/watch?v=abc` goes to `evil.example`, and a card naming `youtube.com` would mislead. Foundation may write a `\` in an `href` as `%5C`, so the iPhone tests compare `href`s with every `\` written as `%5C` on both sides. The card's host line is the parsed host.

`title` is the link's text when it differs from `href`; otherwise `YouTube video` or `Vimeo video` for those kinds, and for the others the path's last segment (the file name; the card shows the host on its own line), percent-decoded as UTF-8 (kept as written when that fails). A link with empty text (`[](https://...)`) is not pinned: the web client gives its `href` as the text (so the file name is the title), while Foundation drops it and nothing is shown. `href` is the link's `href` unchanged.

Clients show a card: a glyph for the kind, the title (at most two lines) and the host, on the code block's surface with a hairline border and 12 pt corners, the full width of the reply. Nothing is fetched before a tap (no thumbnails, previews or icons). On the web every card is a link that opens in a new tab. On the iPhone a `video` or `audio` card plays in place when tapped and stops when it scrolls away; the others open in Safari.

Files. `kinds.json` pins each kind, titles, a thumbnail image inside a link (the link decides), capitals, query and fragment, spaces, images alone in their paragraph, and cards inside lists and quotes; `not-media.json` links that stay links (inside prose, two in a paragraph, other schemes, addresses that are no media, a `\` or `%5C` before the path, a host the URL parser reads differently, emphasis, headings, images beside text).

## Queue (`queue/*.json`)

Each file has `name`, `session` (what the server returns for a session: `state`, optional `terminal` and `queue` as in `SessionDetail`), optionally `send: {error}` (a direct send the server refused), `add: {error}` (an add to the queue the server refused) or `delete: {error}` (a delete the server refused), and `expect`, what both clients show: `composer` `{action, label}`, `queue` `{visible, state?, line?, resume?}` and `items` `[{id, text, state, label, canEdit, canMove, canDelete}]`, plus `keepText` and `message` for a refused request. `composer` is the state after the refusal, if any. Rules, one bullet each:

- Composer. The primary action is `send` labeled "Send" when the session is free: `state` is not `busy` and, when `terminal` is present, it can take typing (`canType` true) and is not `working`. It is `queue` labeled "Add to queue" (the fixtures' name for the action; both clients show the same send arrow, with the accessibility label "Send when Claude finishes") when the session is working (`state` `busy`, or `terminal.working`), blocked (`terminal.canType` false, such as `reason` `mac_in_use` or `disabled`; the Mac decides when to send), or its queue is sending (an item `sending` or `answering` in any queue state, or the queue `running` with items `waiting`: the server answers a direct send `409 busy` then, so a new message keeps its place behind them), and after a direct send was refused with `409 busy`; that offer lasts until the next session detail or event says the session is free. `terminal.status` `unknown` is treated like a terminal that cannot take typing, with no reason: "Add to queue".
- Queue section. `visible` is true only when `queue.items` is not empty (an empty queue is never shown). Both clients fold it to one line ("2 queued · next: …") that a tap opens; a paused queue's `line` and Resume show either way. `state` is the queue's. Paused: `line` is `queue.reason` verbatim (a `note` is ignored) and `resume` is true (a Resume button; only Resume runs a paused queue, moving or editing items never does). Running: `line` is `queue.note` verbatim when there is one (a `reason` is ignored) (for example "Waiting: you're using this session on your Mac", or "Waiting: Claude is working" while the next item waits for Claude to finish, `working-terminal.json`), else absent; `resume` is false.
- Items, in the order given. `label` by state: `waiting` "Waiting", `sending` "Sending", `answering` "Answer in progress". `canEdit` and `canMove` only for `waiting` (a sending or answering item is the first and is never edited or moved). Items with state `done` (the server's answer to a retried add; empty text) are never shown. `canDelete` for `waiting`, and for `sending` or `answering` only while the queue is `paused` (the server answers `409 item_sending` otherwise, so clients hide or disable Delete; if the request is made anyway, the fixed client message is "This message is being sent and can't be changed.").
- Refused requests. After `409 busy` the clients add the message to the queue by themselves and the primary action becomes "Add to queue"; only if that add is refused too does the text stay (`keepText`). A refused add keeps the text in the composer (`keepText`) and shows a fixed `message`: `bad_text` "This message can't be queued (it starts with ! or /, holds control characters, or is too long)."; `queue_full` "The queue is full (20 messages). Delete one to add another." These two and the delete message are client strings, not the server's.
- Offer. `send-refused-busy.json` has `expect.offer` `{action, label, keepText, message}`: after `409 busy` the primary action is "Add to queue" and no `message` is shown (`null`); `keepText` is the text's place while the clients queue it by themselves.
- Reasons. `paused-*.json` has one file per fixed pause reason the server can give, with a realistic `terminal` object for the reasons that concern the Mac's terminal; clients show the server's text unchanged and never rewrite it.

## highlight/

Syntax colours for code blocks. Each file has `name`, `lang` (the fence's info string, matched case-insensitively), `code` and `tokens`, a list of `[kind, text]` whose texts join back to `code` exactly; neighbouring tokens of one kind are merged and empty ones dropped. Kinds: `plain`, `keyword`, `string`, `comment`, `number`, `function`, `key`, `added`, `removed`, `meta`. Languages and aliases: `go`/`golang`; `swift`; `js`, `javascript`, `jsx`, `mjs`, `ts`, `typescript`, `tsx`; `py`/`python`; `sh`, `bash`, `zsh`, `shell`, `console`; `json`; `yaml`/`yml`; `diff`/`patch`. Any other language, or none, is one `plain` token. Rules, scanned left to right: a line comment (`//` for Go, Swift and JS; `#` for Python, shell and YAML; none for JSON) runs to the end of its line; a block comment `/* ... */` (Go, Swift, JS) runs to its close or the end; a string opens with one of the language's quotes (Go `" ' \``; Swift `"`; JS `" ' \``; Python, shell and YAML `" '`; JSON `"`), a backslash escapes the next character except in a backtick string, a backtick string may cross lines and others end at their line's end if unclosed; in JSON a string followed by optional spaces and `:` is a `key`; in YAML, at a line's start, after indentation and an optional `- `, a name of letters, digits, `_ . / -` followed by `:` and a space or line end is a `key`; in shell `$NAME` and `${...}` are `key`; a number starts with a digit not preceded by a letter, digit or `_` and continues over `0-9 A-F a-f x X . _`; a word (`[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`) is a `keyword` when in the language's list (see `highlight.mjs`), else a `function` when the next character is `(`, else `plain`. A diff is read by line: `+++`, `---` and `@@` lines are `meta`, other `+` lines `added`, other `-` lines `removed`, the rest `plain`.
